description: I'm a Computer Science student passionate about AI, machine learning, and space exploration. I have experience in Python, deep learning, and AI-powered applications. I'm looking for creative, collaborative teammates with skills in astronomy, physics, data science, design, or web development to build something impactful together!
summary:
Before astronauts drive or walk at the Moon Base, NASA rehearses on Earth, at analog sites chosen mostly because they are famous. SIMILITUDE asks the engineer's question instead: which test results will actually transfer?
One formula runs on NASA data from both worlds (LRO LOLA/PGDA 78, MRO CTX and CRISM, SWIM; Copernicus DEM, NASA EMIT, MODIS, ERA5-Land). Every site gets a verdict per test variable: TRANSFERS (test it in the field), NO-ANALOG (use a named facility) or UNOBSERVED (measure on site).
The famous sites do not match. 76% of the Moon Base ridge is steeper than 8°; at six classic analog sites the median is 9%, and none of their 54 footprints matches the ridge or any of the five Artemis III candidate regions NASA maps at 5 m. SIMILITUDE finds Earth test terrain for all five, in countries open to NASA. For the ridge, two sites pass every terrain test on two elevation models: Argentina (1 of 1,000 random cells) and Baffin Island, with 71 days of polar-like low Sun.
Checked against NASA and a real rover: our slopes match NASA's maps to 0.0009° and Perseverance's measured tilt at 708 stops (ρ = 0.80). Every test is pre-registered; failures are published.
details:
The problem. NASA rehearses rovers, EVA traverses and landing sensors at Earth analog sites before they fly. Those sites were picked for fame and looks. Nobody checks, per test, whether a result obtained there will still hold at the Moon Base.

What it does. SIMILITUDE is a proving-ground finder. An engineer picks a mission test (touchdown and traverse, low-Sun navigation, Mars rover terrain, Mars ice under dry soil) and a target region. The web app returns the 4 km places on Earth that match, and a card per site: which test results TRANSFER, which need a named facility (NO-ANALOG: reduced-gravity rig, thermal-vacuum chamber), and which orbit cannot judge (UNOBSERVED). A dedicated page covers the Artemis III candidate regions and builds the smallest campaign for each.

How it works. The same code computes the same descriptors on both worlds: slope distribution at a 30 m baseline, roughness, terrain shadow, simulated rover traverses (a slope-limited planner), spectral band depths and ground-ice conditions. A place counts only if it beats a pre-registered random sample of 1,000 Earth cells and holds under three test configurations; terrain leads must also hold on a second independent elevation model (NASADEM or ArcticDEM).

What we found. Famous analog sites under-test slopes: 76% of the Moon Base ridge is steeper than 8°, against a median of 9% at six classic sites, and 0 of their 54 footprints match the ridge or any of the five Artemis III regions NASA maps at 5 m. SIMILITUDE finds Earth test terrain for all five in countries open to NASA. For the ridge, Argentina (the only one of 1,000 random cells to pass) and Baffin Island (71 days a year with every daylight minute below 7°, the closest Earth comes to polar light) pass every terrain test on two elevation models. On Mars, classic analogs match Perseverance's Jezero delta front 42% of the time vs 19% for random land (p = 0.0004). For a crewed-landing candidate in Arcadia Planitia, no Earth site has both the flat plain and the ground ice, so a base rehearsal needs two sites (exploratory).

Why trust it. Our slopes match NASA's own PGDA 78 slope maps to 0.0009° and the tilt Perseverance measured at 708 waypoints (ρ = 0.80). 102 of 109 terrain verdicts hold on a second elevation model. Every test is registered in git before it runs, and every failure is published: our mineral test failed its stop rule, so we publish no mineral site, and every card reports slope and traverse separately because a slope match is not automatically a traverse match.

Impact. Field campaigns cost months and real money. SIMILITUDE tells a test team where a rehearsal will transfer, and where it should not even go (use a facility instead). It answers the test question behind NASA's 2026 Civil Space Shortfalls 1.05 (crew mobility for lunar traverses), 3.02 (landing at south-pole sites in varied illumination), 3.03 (touchdown on sloped terrain) and 16.01 (autonomous surface mobility).

Creativity. We judge an analog the way an engineer judges a wind-tunnel model: by which results transfer, not by how it looks. The method is planet-agnostic: the same code ran on the Moon and Mars without changes.

Tools. Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Rasterio, Matplotlib), Google Earth Engine, NASA earthaccess, OpenAlex API, JavaScript with Leaflet and NASA GIBS, GitHub Actions and Pages. Open source, Apache-2.0.

Factors we considered. Scientific honesty (pre-registered thresholds; every rule changed after seeing data is listed). Usability (plain labels, units, a guide page). Access (countries closed to NASA are flagged). Resolution (30 m slopes cannot see metre-scale boulders; cards say "survey on site"). A verdict feeds a project's own "relevant environment" definition; it assigns no TRL.
